newsitem.title: USA: IBM still sees strong outlook for year.
newsitem.headline: IBM still sees strong outlook for year.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp Chief Financial Officer G. Richard Thoman said he is still "very comfortable" about the computer giant's prospects for 1996 and with its position going forward.
"I feel very good about the quarter and very good about the year," Thoman told an analyst meeting and conference call to discuss the company's third quarter.
Thoman told analysts that the company's third quarter earnings of $2.45 a share had a negative impact of about $0.08 a share from currency fluctuations.

If current spot rates remain stable, Thoman said, he expects currency to continue to negatively impact earnings in the fourth quarter. He said he expects the impact in the fourth quarter to be slightly greater than the third quarter impact, but not as large as the second quarter hit of $0.33 a share.
"It's a minor irritant," Thoman said about currency fluctuations.

Thoman also said that the company was very pleased with its performance in computer hardware, especially in its mainframe business. Even though price declines are still leading to lower mainframe revenues, Thoman said, installations have grown 25 percent.
"We have not seen this kind of growth since the 1991 period," Thoman said. "We are almost back to 1980s growth rates in mainframes."

Thoman also pointed out that a growing proportion of mainframe revenues are now being shipped under services contracts, so that IBM does not get the full sales in a quarter for all its machines shipped.
He also pointed out that IBM's computer services business is still a very strong business and that IBM's services profit margins fell in the quarter because of its additional hiring.
Thoman also said that the company's personal computer business had its best quarter since he has been with IBM, and that the company gained in market share and in gross margins.

In comparing the PC unit's performance to Compaq Computer Corp, Thoman said that IBM tied Compaq in revenue growth, but its profit margins were not better than those of the industry leader. Compaq had Q3 margins of 23.8 percent.
"We materially closed the gap (on Compaq)," Thoman said. "I feel better about the PC company...because of the improvement in gross profit margins."
IBM recently formed a new business unit, aimed at developing product solutions for this growing market.

Thoman also said that the continued industry-wide decline in computer memory chip prices (known as dynamic random access memory chips, or DRAMs), resulted in a $200-$300 million negative impact on semiconductor revenues in the quarter.

Previously, Thoman had forecast that the drop in DRAM pricing would have a positive impact on IBM as its PC business is a big consumer of memory chips. But he said that the negative pricing trend would continue into fourth quarter, with a negative impact on IBM's semiconductor revenues.
